BMC Oral Health
Enhancing furcation involvement 
classification on panoramic radiographs 
with vision transformers
Xuan Zhang1*†, Enting Guo2†, Xu Liu1, Hong Zhao3, Jie Yang1, Wen Li4, Wenlei Wu1* and Weibin Sun1* 
Abstract 
Background  The severity of furcation involvement (FI) directly affected tooth prognosis and influenced treatment 
approaches. However, assessing, diagnosing, and treating molars with FI was complicated by anatomical and mor-
phological variations. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) enhanced diagnostic accuracy for detecting FI 
and measuring furcation defects. Despite its advantages, the high cost and radiation dose associated with CBCT 
equipment limited its widespread use. The aim of this study was to evaluate the performance of the Vision Trans-
former (ViT) in comparison with several commonly used traditional deep learning (DL) models for classifying molars 
with or without FI on panoramic radiographs.
Methods  A total of 1,568 tooth images obtained from 506 panoramic radiographs were used to construct the data-
base and evaluate the models. This study developed and assessed a ViT model for classifying FI from panoramic 
radiographs, and compared its performance with traditional models, including Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Visual 
Geometry Group (VGG)Net, and GoogLeNet.
Results  Among the evaluated models, the ViT model outperformed all others, achieving the highest precision (0.98), 
recall (0.92), and F1 score (0.95), along with the lowest cross-entropy loss (0.27) and the highest accuracy (92%). 
ViT also recorded the highest area under the curve (AUC) (98%), outperforming the other models with statistically 
significant differences (p < 0.05), confirming its enhanced classification capability. The gradient-weighted class activa-
tion mapping (Grad-CAM) analysis on the ViT model revealed the key areas of the images that the model focused 
on during predictions.
Conclusion  DL algorithms can automatically classify FI using readily accessible panoramic images. These findings 
demonstrate that ViT outperforms the tested traditional models, highlighting the potential of transformer-based 
approaches to significantly advance image classification. This approach is also expected to reduce both the radiation 
dose and the financial burden on patients while simultaneously improving diagnostic precision.
Keywords  Vision transformer, Furcation involvement, Deep learning, Panoramic radiograph

Introduction
Furcation involvement (FI) refers to bone loss between 
the roots of a tooth, often caused by bacterial infec-
tion and periodontal disease [1]. Molars with FI are at a 
higher risk of further deterioration, with the severity of FI 
directly affecting the long-term prognosis of the affected 
teeth. In 1953, Glickman introduced a classification 
system for FI [2]. Grade I FI is an early stage with mini-
mal bone loss, usually undetectable on X-rays. Grade II 
FI involves partial bone loss in multi-rooted teeth, with 
some bone and periodontal ligament still intact, and 
may appear as slight widening of the periodontal liga-
ment or minor bone density changes on X-rays. Grades 
III and IV represent advanced FI stages, which appear on 
X-rays as dark spaces between the roots. Research sug-
gests that teeth with Grade I FI have a prognosis similar 
to teeth without FI, while Grades II to IV are associated 
with a higher risk of tooth loss [3]. Grade I cases are typi-
cally managed successfully with subgingival scaling and 
root planing, while Grades II and above often require 
surgical procedures with bone grafts to achieve optimal 
outcomes [4]. The prognosis largely depends on the FI’s 
location and severity: for example, non-surgical treat-
ment leads to a 99–100% survival rate for Grade I molars 
over 5–12 years, whereas this drops to 25% for Grade III 
molars [5].
The treatment approach for multi-rooted teeth relies 
heavily on an accurate diagnosis of FI, as this is essen-
tial for predicting the tooth’s prognosis and choosing the 
best treatment plan [6]. Various tools are used to detect 
FI, including dental probes, periapical radiography, pano-
ramic radiographs, and cone-beam computed tomogra-
phy (CBCT). Among these, panoramic radiographs are 
commonly used in clinical settings, particularly for rou-
tine screenings or when patients present with diverse 
dental concerns. Although they may not be the primary 
choice for detailed periodontal diagnosis, they are often 
employed as an initial screening tool to provide a broad 
overview of dental health [7, 8]. It provides a broad over-
view of the patient’s oral anatomy, including bone loss 
and FI [9]. On X-rays, FI often appears as darker areas 
between the roots, which may indicate either a widened 
periodontal ligament or visible lesions [10]. However, 
the inherent lack of detail and sharpness in panoramic 
radiographs contributes to the difficulty in diagnosing FI, 
especially when root structures overlap or are positioned 
closely together [11].
Numerous studies on artificial intelligence (AI) have 
been conducted in dentistry, inspired by the application 
of AI systems in medicine for disease diagnosis and treat-
ment planning [12]. Traditional models like multi-layer 
perceptrons (MLP) provide a straightforward, fully con-
nected architecture that serves as a useful baseline [13]. 
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), known for their 
hierarchical feature extraction, have been successful in 
detecting and classifying impacted supernumerary teeth 
[14], detecting vertical root fracture on panoramic radi-
ography [15] and determining periodontal bone loss pat-
terns and furcation defects from dental radiographs [16]. 
However, CNNs can be limited in capturing long-range 
dependencies across images [17].
Transformer-based architectures, such as the Vision 
Transformer (ViT), offer an alternative approach by 
dividing images into patches and processing them 
sequentially [18]. Originally developed for natural lan-
guage processing, ViT-based models excel at capturing 
global context and long-range dependencies. While pre-
vious studies have demonstrated their effectiveness in 
various medical imaging tasks [19–21], their application 
to dental radiographs, particularly for FI classification, 
remains largely underexplored.
This study aimed to compare the performance of three 
types of models—MLP, CNNs (e.g., GoogleNet and 
VGGNet), and ViT—in classifying molars with or with-
out FI on panoramic radiographs. By evaluating these 
approaches, the study sought to identify the most effec-
tive model for accurately identifying FI and to inform 
model selection for dental radiograph analysis.
Materials and methods
Data acquisition and preprocessing
Standard reference generation
Panoramic radiographs of 1,089 patients with or with-
out FI from the Nanjing Stomatological Hospital’s image 
database were retrospectively reviewed for the period 
between January 2020 and May 2022. The patients’ ages 
ranged from 25 to 70. All images were obtained using the 
same radiographic device (Orthopantomograph OP 200 
D, Instrumentarium Dental, Tuusula, Finland). Among 
these patients, 506 also underwent CBCT examinations, 
performed with the 3D Accuitomo F17 (Morita, Kyoto, 
Japan) and NewTom VGI EVO (NewTom, Verona, Italy) 
devices. The CBCT scans were acquired using a stand-
ardized protocol for three-dimensional implant planning, 
with a medium field of view (FOV) of either 100 × 55 mm 
or 100 × 90  mm, and a voxel size of 200  μm. The tube 
voltage was set to 90 kV, with a scan time of 12 s. The 
tube current (mA) ranged from 4.5 to 7.1, depending on 
the patient’s skull size and weight. Both maxillary and 
mandibular molars were included in the analysis. Scans 
with severe artifacts caused by metal or implant res-
torations, as well as those with artifacts from post-root 
canal fillings, were excluded. Furthermore, molars with 
root  fusion, caries or those that had undergone filling 
therapy were excluded from the study.

Standard reference for classification task
The experiment extracted 1,568 images of the molar 
region from 506 panoramic radiographs for this study. 
The standard reference for FI classification was verified 
by two periodontists (X.Zh. and X.L.), each with over 
six years of experience in oral clinics. Using the Glick-
man classification, i) Grade 0 or grade I FI: radiographic 
changes are typically absent; ii) Grade II FI: limited wid-
ening of the periodontal ligament or a slight decrease in 
bone density; iii) Grade III or IV FI: radiolucent areas 
between the roots. They reviewed the CBCT images of 
each patient and reached a consensus on the classifica-
tion of FI in maxillary and mandibular molars. Figure 1 
shows cropped panoramic radiographic images and axial 
images reconstructed from CBCT of the same tooth, 
showing different classifications of FI. Consensus classi-
fications were determined through detailed discussions 
between the two periodontists (X.Zh. and X.L.), who 
reviewed the CBCT images and initially provided their 
individual classifications based on the Glickman classi-
fication system. In cases where they could not reach an 
agreement, a third expert (J.Y.), with extensive experience 
in oral periodontology, was consulted to help resolve dis-
crepancies and facilitate a final consensus.
To address radiological similarities, we categorized 
lesion grades in this study as follows: Grade 0 and Grade 
I lesions, which typically lack radiographic changes, were 
classified as Class A and served as the control group 
(negative). Grade II lesions were classified as Class B, 
while Grade III and Grade IV lesions were grouped as 
Class C (positive). The dataset includes 342 maxillary 
molar images and 282 mandibular molar images in Class 
A; 371 maxillary molar images and 251 mandibular molar 
images in Class B; and 143 maxillary molar images and 
179 mandibular molar images in Class C. The methodol-
ogy of this study is illustrated in Fig. 2.
Preprocessing
During preprocessing, images of various sizes were 
resized to 224 × 224 pixels using bilinear interpolation. 
This method interpolates within the nearest 2 × 2 pixel 
neighborhood, preserving both the aspect ratio and 
image details. Following resizing, the images were nor-
malized by scaling pixel values to the range (0, 1). This 
normalization ensures consistent input for the neural 
network and enhances training efficiency by mitigating 
the effects of varying pixel intensities.
Dataset
To enhance the diversity of the dataset, the current study 
employed real-time data augmentation techniques dur-
ing the training process. This study applied a 4 × data 
augmentation, meaning that each original image was 
augmented to produce four additional versions, resulting 
in a total dataset size of five times the original. Therefore, 
the dataset increased from 1,568 images to 7,840 images 
after augmentation. These techniques included ran-
dom rotations, zooming, horizontal flipping, and shear 
transformations, which were applied randomly to each

Training dataset
The identification of furcation defects in panoramic radi-
ographs is a nuanced task that requires the consideration 
of various anatomical and pathological features of the 
first molar. For training the model of this task, we uti-
lized a dataset consisting of panoramic radiographs that 
encompass a broad spectrum of furcation defect presen-
tations. This experiment employed the ViT model, which 
is well-suited for capturing the detailed patterns in the 
images. The model parameters were iteratively updated 
using backpropagation and gradient descent algorithms. 
This iterative process, repeated over multiple epochs, 
allowed the model to progressively refine its ability to 
identify the relevant features within the images.
Validation dataset
The validation dataset was essential for fine-tuning the 
model’s hyperparameters, including the number of lay-
ers, neurons per layer, learning rates, and regularization 
techniques. By systematically adjusting these hyperpa-
rameters and evaluating the model’s performance on the 
validation set, we identified the configuration that opti-
mally balanced model complexity and generalization 
ability. To further enhance the robustness, we employed 
cross-validation, which provided a more thorough assess-
ment of the model’s performance and ensured that it was 
not excessively tuned to a specific data subset. Addition-
ally, early stopping was implemented to prevent overfit-
ting by terminating training once performance on the 
validation set ceased to improve.
Test dataset
The test dataset was reserved for the final evaluation of 
the trained model’s performance. This dataset was used 
to assess the model’s accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 
score, providing a comprehensive understanding of its 
classification capabilities. Additionally, we analyzed the 
receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and cal-
culated the area under the curve (AUC) to evaluate the 
model’s ability to discriminate between different thresh-
old settings. ROC analysis facilitated an understanding 
of the trade-offs between sensitivity and specificity. The 
results from the test dataset offered an unbiased esti-
mate of the model’s performance on unseen data, pro-
viding a realistic measure of its potential application in 
diagnosing furcation defects. By systematically training, 
validating, and testing model, we ensured that it not only 
achieved accuracy on the training data but also general-
ized well to unseen cases. This evaluation process high-
lights the model’s reliability and potential effectiveness in 
clinical applications.
Cross‑validation method
Given the complexity of the task, it was important to 
maximize the effective use of the dataset. To achieve 
this, we employed a stratified cross-validation method, 
which provided robust and reliable performance met-
rics. The dataset was divided into six parts: four were 
used for training, one for validation, and one for testing. 
Each part maintained the class distribution consistent 
with the overall dataset: 624 images for Class A, 622 for 
Class B, and 322 for Class C. The stratified cross-valida-
tion ensured that each subset preserved a representative 
balance of classes across training, validation, and testing 
sets. During the cross-validation process, different com-
binations of these parts were used to train and validate 
the model preventing overfitting.
Figure 4 illustrates the cross-validation process, where 
the dataset was systematically partitioned into multiple 
subsets, allowing us to average the results from differ-
ent combinations of training, validation, and testing sets. 
This approach ensured that the performance metrics 
were based on a comprehensive evaluation of the model 
across various portions of the data, thus reducing the 
risk of overfitting to any particular subset. By employing 
this cross-validation strategy, we obtained performance 
estimates that were consistent across different data par-
titions, helping to identify model configurations that gen-
eralized well to unseen data. This methodical approach 
contributed to the reliability of the model’s performance 
metrics, providing a clearer understanding of how the 
model would perform in real-world applications.
DL architecture
The current study selected several models and compared 
their performances through training, aiming to identify 
the model with the best performance.
MLP
The MLP is a foundational neural network architecture 
comprising multiple layers of neurons, typically including 
an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output 
layer [22]. Activation functions in the hidden layers intro-
duce non-linearity, enabling the model to learn complex 
patterns. The input layer receives preprocessed images,

which pass through the hidden layers. The output layer 
uses a softmax function to produce probabilities for the 
target classes, and the predicted probabilities are com-
pared to the true labels to calculate.
CNN
CNNs are deep learning models ideal for image pro-
cessing, as they capture spatial hierarchies in visual data 
through layers of convolutional filters, pooling, and fully 
connected layers. Convolutional layers learn features like 
edges and textures, while pooling layers reduce spatial 
dimensions to retain essential features with lower com-
putational demands [23]. The VGGNet model uses 3 × 3 
convolutional kernels to capture detailed and hierarchi-
cal patterns, making it effective in analyzing both struc-
tural and fine-grained image features [24]. GoogleNet, by 
introducing inception modules with multiple filters sizes, 
captures diverse patterns at different scales, enhancing 
recognition capabilities and computational efficiency by 
reducing parameters while maintaining high accuracy 
[25].
Vision Transformer (ViT)
The ViT represents a novel approach to image classifica-
tion by leveraging the transformer architecture, which 
was originally developed for natural language process-
ing [26]. In this approach, an image is partitioned into a 
sequence of fixed-size patches, each measuring 16 × 16 
pixels. These patches are linearly embedded into a 
768-dimensional vector space, and positional embed-
dings are added to preserve spatial information. The 
sequence of embedded patches is then input into a trans-
former encoder consisting of 12 layers.
Each layer of the transformer encoder incorporates a 
multi-head self-attention mechanism with 12 attention 
heads and a feed-forward neural network. The self-atten-
tion mechanism enables the model to dynamically weigh 
the significance of each patch relative to others, thereby 
capturing long-range dependencies and contextual 
relationships within the image. Mathematically, the self-

In this specific implementation, the input image is

16 × 16 patches, resulting in 196 patches per image. These 
patches are processed through the 12 transformer lay-

sub-layers, followed by layer normalization. The output 
from the final transformer layer is passed through a clas-
sification head, where a softmax function is applied to 
generate probability distributions over the target classes.

To optimize ViT training, a cosine annealing learning 
rate schedule was applied, starting with a high learning 
rate that gradually decreases along a cosine curve. This 
strategy prevents premature convergence to local min-
ima and allows for finer adjustments, enhancing overall 
model convergence. Gradient clipping was used along-
side learning rate scheduling to maintain stable train-
ing for the ViT model by capping gradients to prevent 
the exploding gradient problem, which is essential for 
deep transformer models. This approach ensures stable 
updates during backpropagation, avoiding destabilization 
in training.

Statistical analysis
All data were organized and analyzed using IBM 
SPSS® Statistics, Version 23. To evaluate the agreement 
between the classifications of the two observers, Cohen’s 
κ (Cohen, 1960) was calculated. The McNemar χ2 test 
was employed to assess any disagreements between the 
observers. Additionally, cross-validation was applied 
to maximize the utilization of the dataset, allowing for 
a more robust assessment of the model’s performance 
across different subsets of data. Paired t-tests conducted 
on the AUC scores from each cross-validation fold 
revealed significant differences in AUC between the MLP 
model and the other models (p < 0.001).
Result
Cohen’s κ value for the interobserver agreement between 
the two observers was 0.932 (> 0.75). This indicated that 
the two observers’ classifications were not significantly 
different. The number of molars with varying degrees of 
FI did not influence the agreement (Pearson correlation: 
p = 0.180).

The study assessed the performance of several DL 
models using metrics like precision, recall, F1 score, 
cross-entropy loss, and accuracy (Table 1). GoogleNet 
and VGGNet showed strong performance, especially 
in precision (0.94 ± 0.026 and 0.96 ± 0.023) and F1 
score (0.91 ± 0.024 and 0.93 ± 0.024), indicating effec-
tive identification of positive cases. However, the ViT 
model outperformed all others, with the highest pre-
cision (0.98 ± 0.012), recall (0.92 ± 0.039), and F1 score 
(0.95 ± 0.023), as well as the lowest cross-entropy loss 
(0.27 ± 0.054) and highest accuracy (92% ± 2.540). These 
results highlight the ViT model as the most balanced 
and effective in classification.

(precision 0.95 ± 0.023, recall 0.90 ± 0.029, F1 score 
0.92 ± 0.023, 
cross-entropy

89 ± 2.598%). MLP had relatively lower performance, 
with precision of 0.89 ± 0.020, recall of 0.83 ± 0.032, F1 
score of 0.86 ± 0.020, cross-entropy of 0.51 ± 0.051, and 
accuracy of 82 ± 2.569%.
In summary, the ViT model demonstrated the highest 
accuracy and effectiveness for both maxillary and man-
dibular molar classification tasks, followed closely by 
VGGNet and GoogLeNet, while MLP showed compara-

suggest that ViT may be the most suitable model for 
accurately classifying molar features in this study.

Discussion
FI occurs when bone loss reaches the area between the 
roots of multi-rooted teeth. FI classifications are typically 
based on the depth and extent of attachment loss. How-
ever, diagnosing and treating molars with FI is often chal-
lenging due to the complex variations in tooth anatomy 
[27]. Although CBCT imaging improves FI detection 
and provides detailed measurements of defects, its high 
cost and radiation dose limit its routine use in clinics 
[28]. Although panoramic radiographs are not ideal for 
detailed periodontal diagnosis, they are sometimes used 
as an initial screening tool. However, their limited detail 
and sharpness make diagnosing FI challenging, especially 
when root structures overlap or are closely positioned. 
The current study evaluated four advanced CNN models, 
with CBCT images as a standard reference, to classify FI 
in molars based on panoramic radiographs from patients 
with chronic periodontitis. Among these models, the 
Vision ViT showed the best performance, demonstrating 
the potential of CNNs to assist clinicians in diagnosing 
FI more efficiently using panoramic radiographs. This 
approach could reduce patient costs and lower radiation 
exposure by minimizing the need for CBCT.
Radiographic assessments of FI are often complicated 
by the complex structure of molars and the overlap-
ping of anatomical features. In a review of radiographic 
parameters, Brägger noted that it becomes harder to 
accurately assess FI on radiographs when the cemento-
enamel junction and root tips are not clearly visible [29]. 
Accurate FI detection depends on identifying the furca-
tion area and the periodontal ligament space, which can 
be difficult when dealing with the anatomy of back teeth 
and overlapping structures. Additionally, variations in 
imaging factors—such as operator technique and equip-
ment settings—can further impact image clarity. There-
fore, to achieve accurate FI diagnosis, it’s important to 
consider the remaining bone support and the tooth root 
structure as part of a comprehensive evaluation [30].
Previous studies have shown that AI is effective in clas-
sifying FI from panoramic radiographs. Kurt-Bayrakdar 
et  al. used DL algorithms and segmentation methods 
to detect bone resorption patterns, demonstrating that 
CNNs can automatically assess periodontal disease 
severity [16]. Lee et al. used machine learning to analyze 
electronic health records and predict factors contribut-
ing to tooth loss, including grade II and III FI. Mao et al. 
evaluated FI in molars with periapical radiographs and 
DL, highlighting AI’s potential in dental diagnosis [31]. 
Collectively, these studies suggest that AI methods can 
predict and classify FI using two-dimensional imaging. 
One of the key advantages of ViT is its ability to model 
global context more effectively than traditional CNNs, 
which primarily focus on local features through convo-
lution operations. This global perspective enables ViT to 
capture intricate patterns and dependencies that might 
be overlooked by CNN-based models.
This study assessed the performance of various DL 
models using metrics like precision, recall, F1 score, 
cross-entropy loss, and accuracy. The ViT outperformed 
other models, showing high precision, recall, and accu-
racy, along with the lowest cross-entropy loss. It demon-
strated fast and stable convergence, surpassing models 
like VGGNet, GoogleNet, and MLP, which had lower 
accuracy. ViT also achieved the highest AUC with statis-
tically significant improvements, highlighting its superior 
classification ability. Grad-CAM analysis of ViT revealed 
key image areas used in predictions, confirming its effec-
tiveness for image classification. Our findings demon-
strate that the ViT not only matches but often surpasses 
traditional CNN architectures in terms of accuracy. This 
underscores the transformative potential of transformer-
based models in advancing the field of image classifi-
cation. This is particularly apparent in medical image 
analysis, where accurate modeling of complex patterns is 
essential.
AI algorithms are increasingly employed in digital 
healthcare, particularly for image and text recognition 
tasks. Among these, the ViT has emerged as a leading 
algorithm, often replacing or complementing traditional 
techniques such as CNNs. For example, Tang et al. uti-
lized ViT to automatically segment brain tumors and 
measure lesion sizes in CT images, illustrating its effec-
tiveness in medical imaging [32]. Similarly, Li et  al. 
applied ViT to dental applications, specifically for seg-
menting root canals in X-ray images [33]. Additionally, 
Zhao et al. developed the TraSeTR algorithm, based on 
ViT, which uses tracking cues to enhance the segmenta-
tion of surgical instruments, thereby improving cognitive

intelligence in robot-assisted surgeries. These advance-
ments underscore ViT’s versatility and its growing influ-
ence across various areas of digital healthcare [34].
The advancements and innovations in this work: (1) 
This study employed the ViT in the model training, 
which offers advantages such as better capture of global 
context and improved scalability compared to traditional 
CNNs. (2) This study used cross-validation and imple-
mented Gradient Clipping to enhance data utilization, 
which reduces the risk of overfitting and stabilizes the 
training process.
There are some limitations in the current study that 
warrant attention. Firstly, although this model per-
formed well on the current dataset, the dataset’s scale 
and diversity may not adequately capture the complexi-
ties of real-world applications. Future studies should 
aim to expand the dataset’s size and diversity to better 
validate the model’s generalizability. Secondly, while the 
ViT model exhibited excellent performance, its compu-
tational complexity necessitates substantial resources, 
which could be a challenge in resource-constrained envi-
ronments. Future research should investigate more effi-
cient model architectures or optimization algorithms to 
reduce computational costs. In terms of future directions 
for improvement, expanding the dataset and enhancing 
data preprocessing could significantly improve the mod-
el’s generalization ability. Exploring more efficient model 
architectures would help in reducing computational costs 
while maintaining high performance, making the model 
more practical for broader applications. Although CBCT 
is recommended as an auxiliary tool for evaluating FI 
[35], intraoperative assessment remains the “gold stand-
ard” [36]. In this study, high AUC values indicate strong 
model performance with CBCT as the reference stand-
ard. However, further research with intraoperative vali-
dation is necessary to confirm these findings. We used 
a CBCT voxel size of 200 µm, balancing resolution with 
radiation safety. While smaller voxel sizes may enhance 
the detection of subtle Fl features, they are often associ-
ated with increased radiation dose due to adjustments 
in other acquisition parameters, such as the number of 
basis images, required to improve image quality [37]. 
The 200 µm voxel size, commonly used in dental imag-
ing, provides adequate resolution for most pathologies 
but may limit detection of subtle FI [38]. Additionally, 
variability in acquisition parameters, such as tube cur-
rent adjustments for patient-specific needs, could affect 
FI visibility and introduce bias [39]. Future studies should 
explore optimal voxel sizes and standardize acquisition 
parameters to improve diagnostic accuracy and repro-
ducibility, while also refining the classification criteria for 
the dataset to enhance model validation. Moreover, self-
reported symptoms such as tooth mobility and sensitivity 
show a strong correlation with FI. Integrating these 
symptoms into the diagnostic model through feature 
encoding could further enhance its accuracy.
Conclusion
The results of this study demonstrate that ViT signifi-
cantly outperforms the tested traditional deep learning 
models in classifying FI using panoramic radiographs, 
indicating its enhanced capability for this task. The find-
ings highlight the potential of the ViT model to improve 
diagnostic accuracy and contribute to the development 
of more effective AI-driven tools in clinical practice, with 
benefits for both patient care and healthcare efficiency.

Abstract: Background The severity of furcation involvement (FI) directly affected tooth prognosis and influenced treatment approaches. However, assessing, diagnosing, and treating molars with FI was complicated by anatomical and mor- phological variations. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) enhanced diagnostic accuracy for detecting FI and measuring furcation defects. Despite its advantages, the high cost and radiation dose associated with CBCT equipment limited its widespread use. The aim of this study was to evaluate the performance of the Vision Trans- former (ViT) in comparison with several commonly used traditional deep learning (DL) models for classifying molars with or without FI on panoramic radiographs. Methods A total of 1,568 tooth images obtained from 506 panoramic radiographs were used to construct the data- base and evaluate the models. This study developed and assessed a ViT model for classifying FI from panoramic radiographs, and compared its performance with traditional models, including Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Visual Geometry Group (VGG)Net, and GoogLeNet. Results Among the evaluated models, the ViT model outperformed all others, achieving the highest precision (0.98), recall (0.92), and F1 score (0.95), along with the lowest cross-entropy loss (0.27) and the highest accuracy (92%). ViT also recorded the highest area under the curve (AUC) (98%), outperforming the other models with statistically significant differences (p < 0.05), confirming its enhanced classification capability. The gradient-weighted class activa- tion mapping (Grad-CAM) analysis on the ViT model revealed the key areas of the images that the model focused on during predictions. Conclusion DL algorithms can automatically classify FI using readily accessible panoramic images. These findings demonstrate that ViT outperforms the tested traditional models, highlighting the potential of transformer-based approaches to significantly advance image classification. This approach is also expected to reduce both the radiation dose and the financial burden on patients while simultaneously improving diagnostic precision.
